source_text: Dictum contra est concedendum esse nunc ista recte non fieri, immo ideo prorsus iam non fieri, quod omnipotenti nunc displicent, uerumtamen placuisse, cum fierent; nos enim nescire, unde tunc placuerint, nunc autem unde displiceant, ++ dum tamen certum sit nec tunc fieri potuisse, nisi placuissent omnipotenti. nec nunc cessasse, nisi displicuissent omnipotenti.. ad hoc ego, cur ergo, inquam, et nunc talia clanculo fiunt, quae uel perpetuo delitiscunt uel deprehensa puniuntur, si nihil horum fieri sinit omnipotens, nisi quod ei iusto placet, cum iusto quod iniustum est placere non possit? contra hoc dictum est nunc omnino talia non fieri. sacra enim illa, inquit, non fiunt, quae pontificalibus conscripta sunt libris; ea quippe tunc recte fiebant, ea tunc deo placere demonstrabantur eo ipso, quod ab omnipotente ac iusto fieri sinebantur; si quid autem nunc prohibitorum sacrificiorum fit occulte atque inlicite, non est illi pontificali sacrificiorum generi conparandum, sed in eodem deputandum, quod etiam nocturno fit tempore, cum haec omnia inlicita ipsis pontificalibus libris certum sit prohiberi atque damnari. hic respondi: cur ergo uel talia permittit deus fieri, si nihil eorum malefactorum contemnit, quae contra religionem fiunt, cum praesertim haec eum curare hinc etiam cogantur concedere, qui pontificales libros magni aestimant, quod ea, quae his libris prohibentur. utique diuinitus prohiberi asserunt? quomodo ergo diuinitus prohibentur, nisi quia displicent deo, quae utique prohibendo non solum sibi displicere, uerum etiam curare se ostendit neque omnino contemnere? unde colligitur, quod deus aliquid et improbet iustus et tamen permittat omnipotens.
thought_title: God can disapprove and yet permit
orientation: Augustine is answering the interlocutors' claim that whatever God permits must please Him, pressing them on why forbidden rites still happen secretly if God permits nothing unjust.
pass_a_gloss: It was said against this that it must be conceded that these things are now rightly not done, indeed that they are now for that very reason no longer done, because they now displease the Almighty, but that they had pleased when they were done; for we do not know why they pleased then, and why they displease now, but nevertheless it is certain that they could not have been done then unless they had pleased the Almighty, and that they would not have ceased now unless they had displeased the Almighty. To this I said: Why then, I said, are such things even now done secretly, which either stay hidden forever or are punished when detected, if the Almighty allows nothing of these things to happen except what pleases Him as the righteous God, since what is unjust cannot please the righteous God? Against this it was said that such things are now not done at all. For those sacred rites, he said, are not done, which are written down in the pontifical books; those indeed were then rightly done, those were then shown to please God by this very fact, that they were allowed to be done by the Almighty and righteous God; but if anything of the forbidden sacrifices is now done secretly and unlawfully, it is not to be compared with that pontifical kind of sacrifices, but is to be counted in the same category as what is also done at night, since it is certain that all these unlawful things are forbidden and condemned by the pontifical books themselves. Here I replied: Why then does God permit even such things to be done, if He despises none of those evil deeds which are done against religion, especially since those who value the pontifical books highly are forced to concede that He cares about these things, because they assert that the things which are forbidden by these books are forbidden by divine authority? How then are they forbidden by divine authority, unless because they displease God, who by forbidding them shows not only that they displease Him, but also that He cares about them and does not despise them at all? From this it is gathered that God as righteous disapproves of something and yet as Almighty permits it.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for God's power to permit or prevent all things.
Fixed glossary term emphasizing God's justice in the argument.
Refers to the pagan Roman priestly books containing ritual regulations; kept literal to preserve the institutional reference.
Fixed glossary term for worship owed to God, here the true religion opposed to pagan rites.
Adverb meaning 'from heaven' or 'by divine power'; rendered as 'by divine authority' to capture the claim that the prohibitions come from God.

pass_b_english: The reply came back that we must concede that these things are rightly not done now—indeed, that they are no longer done at all precisely because they now displease the Almighty—but that they did please him when they were done. We simply do not know why they pleased him then or why they displease him now, but this much is certain: they could not have been done then unless they had pleased the Almighty, and they would not have ceased now unless they had displeased the Almighty.

To this I said: Why, then, do such things still happen secretly even now—things that either stay hidden forever or are punished when they are detected—if the Almighty permits nothing to happen unless it pleases the righteous God, and what is unjust cannot please the righteous God?

The reply came back that such things are not done at all now. Those sacred rites, they said, are not performed—the ones written down in the pontifical books. Those were rightly done then, and they were shown to please God then by the very fact that the Almighty and righteous God allowed them to be done. But if any of the now-forbidden sacrifices is performed secretly and unlawfully, it is not to be compared with that pontifical kind of sacrifice. Rather, it is to be counted in the same category as what is done at night, since it is certain that all these unlawful things are forbidden and condemned by the pontifical books themselves.

Here I responded: Why, then, does God permit even such things to happen, if he does not despise any of the evil deeds that are committed against religion—especially since those who hold the pontifical books in high esteem are forced to concede that God cares about these things, because they assert that what is forbidden in those books is forbidden by divine authority? How are they forbidden by divine authority unless they displease God? By forbidding them, he shows not only that they displease him but also that he cares about them and does not despise them at all. From this it follows that God, as the righteous God, disapproves of something and yet, as the Almighty, permits it.
notes: The source contains '++' before 'dum tamen certum sit', indicating damage or an editorial marker in the text; the gloss proceeds with the following words as they stand.

last_rejected.quote: if he does not despise any of the evil deeds
last_rejected.why: English adds 'evil' not in source; 'malefactorum' = 'of wrongdoers/evildoers' (substantive), not 'evil deeds'
last_rejected.fix: if he does not despise any of those wrongdoers
last_rejected.ruling: 'malefactorum' is genitive plural of 'malefactum' = evil deeds; rendering as 'evil deeds' is standard and correct.

last_rejected.quote: does not despise any of the evil deeds that are committed against religion
last_rejected.why: 'fiunt' = 'are done/occur,' not 'are committed'; phrase modifies the forbidden acts, not 'evil deeds'
last_rejected.fix: any of those wrongdoers whose acts are done against religion
last_rejected.ruling: 'fiunt' = are done; 'committed' is within normal range; relative clause 'quae contra religionem fiunt' modifies 'malefactorum' correctly.

last_rejected.why: Missing clause: 'which they certainly assert are forbidden by divine authority' or similar
last_rejected.fix: because they certainly assert that what is forbidden in those books is forbidden by divine authority
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'utique diuinitus prohiberi asserunt' is rendered in English: 'they assert that what is forbidden... is forbidden by divine authority.' Not omitted.
